Quick Answer

How Do You Convert Hourly Pay to Annual Salary?

To convert hourly pay to annual salary, multiply your hourly wage by the hours you work each week and the weeks you work each year.

The Standard Calculation Formula Annual Salary = Hourly Rate × Hours Worked Per Week × Weeks Worked Per Year
For a standard full-time schedule (40 hours/week × 52 weeks): Annual Salary = Hourly Rate × 40 × 52 (or Hourly Rate × 2,080)
So at $25.00 an hour: $25/hour × 40 hours/week × 52 weeks = $52,000/year

Note: that's gross pay, before federal, state, and local taxes, insurance, or retirement contributions come out.

What Is Hourly Pay?

Before we get into the math, let's pin down a few payroll terms you'll hear from employers, recruiters, and tax folks:

  • Hourly Wage (Hourly Rate): The set amount your employer pays you for each hour you work. If you earn $25.00 for every hour on the clock, your hourly rate is $25.00.
  • Hours Worked: All the hours you put in during a pay period. Full-time jobs usually mean 40 hours a week, but part-time schedules often run from 15 to 35 hours.
  • Gross Earnings: Everything you earn before taxes, payroll withholdings, health care deductions, or retirement contributions come out.
  • Annual Salary: Your total gross pay over a full 12-month calendar year. Salaried folks usually get a fixed annual figure even if their weekly hours wobble a bit, while hourly workers get paid for the exact hours they log.

Your annual income doesn't just come down to your hourly rate. It also depends on how steadily you work through all 52 weeks of the year. Here's how an hourly wage grows into an annual salary:

Wage Progression Flow Standard 40-Hour Baseline
$25.00 / hour  →  40 hours / week  →  52 weeks / year  →  $52,000 / year
1. Base Hourly Wage → 2. Weekly Schedule → 3. Work Weeks → 4. Annual Gross Pay

The Standard 2,080 Hours Baseline Explained

In payroll, HR, and government labor stats across North America, 2,080 hours is the standard full-time baseline:

40 hours per week × 52 weeks per year = 2,080 scheduled hours per year

That's why recruiters and hiring managers use a handy shortcut: just multiply your hourly wage by 2,080:

Hourly Rate × 2,080 = Estimated Annual Salary

Earn $30 an hour? $30 × 2,080 = $62,400 per year. Going the other way, divide a salary by 2,080 to find the hourly rate behind it: $60,000 ÷ 2,080 = $28.85 per hour. You can try your own numbers in our free Salary to Hourly Calculator.

Important E-E-A-T Real-World Note: 2,080 hours is the standard full-time baseline, but your real yearly earnings might look different. If your employer schedules 35 or 37.5 hours a week, or you take unpaid leave, work overtime, or work odd shifts, your actual earnings won't line up with 2,080 hours. Always run your numbers on your real work agreement.

How to Calculate Annual Salary Step by Step

Here are five simple steps to work out your exact annual income:

  1. Step 1: Identify your base hourly pay rate.
    Locate your regular hourly wage on your pay stub, employment contract, or job offer letter. For this walk-through, we'll use $25.00 per hour.
  2. Step 2: Determine your regular weekly hours.
    Work out how many hours you put in during a typical week. For most full-time jobs that's 40 hours per week. Part-time work might be 20, 25, or 30 hours.
  3. Step 3: Determine the number of paid weeks in the year.
    A full calendar year has 52 weeks. If your job includes paid vacation, paid sick time, and paid federal holidays, you get paid for all 52 weeks.
  4. Step 4: Multiply your hourly wage by weekly hours and annual weeks.
    Multiply your rate by your weekly hours to get your weekly gross pay, then multiply by 52:
    $25.00/hour × 40 hours/week = $1,000.00 weekly gross pay
    $1,000.00 × 52 paid weeks = $52,000.00 annual gross salary
  5. Step 5: Adjust for unpaid time off or leave.
    If your job doesn't offer paid time off and you take 2 weeks off over the summer or the holidays, you only work 50 paid weeks:
    $25.00/hour × 40 hours/week × 50 paid weeks = $50,000.00 annual gross salary
    Counting those unpaid weeks keeps your budget honest and shows you what you'll really bring in.

How Work Hours Affect Annual Salary

A lot of people assume everyone works exactly 40 hours a week. In real life, schedules vary a ton across industries, from part-time retail to long manufacturing shifts. And since your annual salary comes straight from your total hours, even a few extra hours a week can shift your yearly pay by thousands.

The table below shows what the same $25.00 per hour rate pays over a year at different weekly hours:

Schedule Type Hours / Week Weeks / Year Total Annual Hours $25.00/hr Annual Pay
Part-Time (Half Time)20 hrs52 wks1,040 hrs$26,000.00
Part-Time (Substantial)30 hrs52 wks1,560 hrs$39,000.00
Standard Full-Time40 hrs52 wks2,080 hrs$52,000.00
Extended Schedule*45 hrs52 wks2,340 hrs$58,500.00*
Heavy Schedule*50 hrs52 wks2,600 hrs$65,000.00*

*Schedules over 40 hours a week usually qualify for overtime pay. Under the FLSA, eligible employees working 45 or 50 hours must be paid 1.5× time and a half for those extra hours, so their real earnings are higher than the straight-time numbers above.

How Unpaid Time Off Changes Annual Pay

A lot of hourly jobs come with no paid vacation or paid sick days. If you take time off for family stuff, travel, illness, or a company holiday shutdown without pay, your annual earnings drop by that amount.

To account for unpaid time off, subtract your unpaid weeks from 52 before you do the math:

Annual Salary = Hourly Rate × Weekly Hours × (52 − Unpaid Weeks)

Here's what unpaid time off does to annual gross pay at $25.00 per hour (40 hours/week):

52 Weeks Paid (Full Year)

40 hours/week · 0 unpaid weeks

$52,000.00 gross / year

Standard baseline compensation

50 Weeks Paid (2 Weeks Unpaid)

40 hours/week · 2 unpaid weeks off

$50,000.00 gross / year

-$2,000.00 reduction in annual earnings

Paid Time Off (PTO) vs. Unpaid Leave: Remember, paid vacation, paid sick leave, and paid company holidays don't cut into your gross annual salary. If you get two weeks of paid vacation, you're still paid for 52 weeks, so your annual gross salary stays at $52,000. Only unpaid time off comes off the total.

How Overtime Affects Annual Income

Under US federal law (the Fair Labor Standards Act) and state labor rules, non-exempt hourly workers who go over 40 hours in a workweek must be paid overtime of at least 1.5 times (time and a half) their regular hourly wage.

Overtime Hourly Rate = Base Hourly Wage × 1.5

Base: $25.00/hour → Overtime Rate: $37.50/hour ($25.00 × 1.5)

When overtime is in the mix, work out your regular hours and overtime hours separately, then add them up:

Total Annual Earnings = (Regular Hours × Base Rate × 52) + (Overtime Hours × Overtime Rate × 52)

Take someone earning $25.00 an hour who works 45 hours a week (40 regular hours + 5 overtime hours) across 52 weeks:

  • Regular Earnings: 40 hours × $25.00 = $1,000.00 per week ($52,000.00 per year)
  • Overtime Earnings: 5 hours × $37.50 = $187.50 per week ($9,750.00 per year)
  • Total Gross Annual Compensation: $1,000.00 + $187.50 = $1,187.50 per week, or $61,750.00 per year

Just 5 extra hours of overtime a week adds nearly $10,000 to your yearly income. You can play around with different overtime hours and multipliers (like 2.0× double time) in our Overtime Calculator.

Gross Salary vs. Take-Home Pay

One thing trips a lot of people up: mixing up your annual gross salary with your actual net take-home pay. A gross salary of $52,000 doesn't mean $52,000 lands in your bank account over the year.

Gross pay is everything you earn before your employer takes out mandatory taxes and any payroll deductions you signed up for. What usually comes off your paycheck:

  • Federal Income Tax: Tax brackets that run from 10% to 37%, depending on your taxable income, filing status (single, married, head of household), and W-4 withholding.
  • FICA Taxes (Social Security & Medicare): The mandatory federal payroll tax, 7.65% in total: 6.2% for Social Security up to the annual wage cap, plus 1.45% for Medicare.
  • State and Local Income Taxes: State income tax runs from 0% (in states like Texas, Florida, Washington, and Nevada) to over 10% in states like California and New York, plus local taxes where they apply.
  • Pre-Tax Employee Benefits: What you put toward health, dental, and vision insurance premiums, Health Savings Accounts (HSA), Flexible Spending Accounts (FSA), and a traditional 401(k).
  • Post-Tax Deductions: Roth 401(k) contributions, union dues, wage garnishments, or life insurance.

Tax brackets, state rates, and insurance premiums vary so much from person to person that no wage converter can give one universal after-tax take-home number without knowing your filing details. To see what deductions do to a single paycheck, try your numbers in our free Paycheck Calculator. And to see where the gap between gross and net actually goes, read our breakdown of gross pay versus net pay, and what actually lands in your account.

Hourly vs. Annual Salary: Which Is Better?

When you're weighing up job offers, you might wonder whether hourly or salaried work is the better deal. Honestly, neither one wins every time. Each comes with its own legal rights, protections, and money perks.

Hourly Pay Model

Job Offer A: Hourly

  • Guaranteed pay for every minute worked
  • Overtime premium (1.5×) over 40 hours
  • Clear separation of work and personal time
  • Unpaid holidays or reduced hours lower income
Base: $25.00/hr · 40 hrs/wk = $52,000/yr
Salaried Model

Job Offer B: Salaried

  • Consistent, predictable monthly paycheck
  • Paid vacation, holidays, and sick days included
  • Health benefits and bonuses often higher
  • Exempt from overtime; 50-hr weeks uncompensated
$55,000/yr salary at 45 hrs/wk = $23.50/hr effective!

Look closer and Job Offer B isn't the winner it seems ($55,000 vs. $52,000). If that salaried job means 45 hours a week with no overtime, your effective hourly rate actually drops to $23.50 an hour. You can compare job offers side by side, commute times and PTO included, with our Salary Comparison Calculator. Common Mistakes When Converting Hourly Pay

Steer clear of these seven traps when you're working out your annual earnings:

Mistake 1: Assuming everyone works exactly 2,080 hours.

Plenty of jobs run on 35, 37.5, or 45 hours a week. If you assume 2,080 hours without checking your offer letter, your yearly figure can be off by thousands of dollars.

Mistake 2: Ignoring unpaid vacation and holiday shutdowns.

If your employer shuts down over Christmas week, or you take two weeks of unpaid summer travel, you'll only be paid for 50 or 51 weeks. Always take unpaid weeks off your 52-week multiplier.

Mistake 3: Counting overtime as guaranteed base salary.

Overtime can be cut whenever management decides. Never plan your rent, mortgage, or everyday bills around overtime pay that isn't guaranteed in writing.

Mistake 4: Confusing gross earnings with take-home pay.

If you budget your rent or car payment off a gross $52,000 salary instead of your after-tax take-home pay, you'll run short.

Mistake 5: Multiplying a biweekly paycheck by 2 to estimate monthly pay.

There are 52 weeks in a year, so you get 26 biweekly paychecks, not 24. Two months a year come with three paychecks instead of two. Multiply a biweekly check by 2 and you'll undercount your annual salary by a whole month's pay.

Mistake 6: Overlooking seasonal hour fluctuations.

In retail, hospitality, landscaping, or construction, hours shoot up in peak season and drop off in slow months. Use a yearly average instead of multiplying your best week by 52.

Mistake 7: Comparing hourly and salary jobs without evaluating benefits.

A $28/hour contract job with no health coverage, no 401(k) match, and no paid time off is often worth less overall than a $25/hour job with solid benefits and 3 weeks of paid leave.

Limitations

  1. Gross pay only: every conversion in this guide is before taxes and deductions. The annual figure is what you earn on paper, not what lands in your bank account.
  2. The 2,080-hour baseline is a convention: it assumes 40 hours a week for 52 fully paid weeks. Part-time schedules, seasonal work, and unpaid leave all produce a different annual total.
  3. Overtime is priced separately: hours past 40 in a week are usually paid at a premium, so a year with regular overtime converts to more than the simple rate-times-hours result.
  4. Salary comparisons are approximate: a salary normally covers paid holidays and PTO, while an hourly wage only pays for hours worked, so the same annual figure can stand for very different amounts of worked time.
  5. Rates change mid-year: a raise or rate change partway through the year splits it into two rates. A single conversion only describes the months worked at that one rate.
  6. Planning estimates: your actual annual pay depends on your employer's payroll calendar and the hours you really work. Use these figures to compare options, not as a pay guarantee.

Frequently Asked Questions

Here are straight answers to the questions people ask most about converting hourly pay to annual salary:

How do I convert hourly pay to annual salary?

Multiply your hourly wage by the hours you work each week, then multiply that by the number of paid weeks you work each year. For a standard full-time schedule of 40 hours a week across 52 weeks (2,080 hours in all), just multiply your hourly rate by 2,080. So $25 an hour times 2,080 hours comes out to an estimated $52,000 a year in gross pay, before taxes and payroll deductions.

How much is $20 an hour per year?

On a standard full-time schedule of 40 hours a week and 52 paid weeks a year (2,080 working hours), $20 an hour works out to $41,600 a year before taxes. That breaks down to roughly $800 gross a week, $1,600 every two weeks across 26 paychecks, or about $3,466.67 a month on average, before deductions. Take 2 weeks of unpaid vacation, so 50 paid weeks, and your annual gross pay drops to $40,000.

How much is $25 an hour per year?

$25 an hour comes to $52,000 a year gross on the usual full-time schedule of 40 hours a week over 52 paid weeks (2,080 hours). That means $1,000 gross a week; $2,000 per check every two weeks across 26 pay periods; and about $4,333.33 a month on average. If you take 2 unpaid weeks off each year, your annual earnings drop to $50,000.

How much is $30 an hour per year?

At 40 hours a week and 52 paid weeks a year, $30 an hour adds up to $62,400 a year gross. That works out to $1,200 a week, $2,400 every two weeks, and an average of $5,200 a month before taxes, health insurance, and retirement contributions. Working part-time at 30 hours a week, $30 an hour comes to $46,800 a year.

How many hours are in a full-time work year?

A standard full-time work year has 2,080 scheduled hours. That number comes from 40 scheduled hours a week times 52 weeks in a year (40 × 52 = 2,080). HR and payroll teams use 2,080 hours as the go-to figure for working out annual pay, paid leave, and what a salary is worth per hour across North America.

Does 2,080 hours always equal a full year's pay?

No. 2,080 hours is the standard full-time payroll benchmark, but your real hours depend on your actual schedule. Unpaid time off, seasonal shifts, a 35- or 45-hour week, or overtime hours all change your paid hours. Leap years or certain pay calendars can also have 2,088 or 2,096 working hours.

Does overtime change annual salary?

Yes, and by a lot. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), non-exempt employees who work more than 40 hours in a workweek usually get 1.5 times their regular hourly rate for each overtime hour. Say you earn $25 an hour and work 5 overtime hours every week: that adds an extra $9,750 a year, taking your total gross annual pay from $52,000 to $61,750.

Does unpaid vacation reduce annual income?

Yes. If your job doesn't offer paid time off (PTO) and you take unpaid vacation or time away from work, every unpaid week comes straight off your gross annual earnings. Two unpaid weeks, for example, cut your paid weeks from 52 to 50. At $25 an hour and 40 hours a week, those two unpaid weeks cost you $2,000 a year, dropping your earnings from $52,000 to $50,000.

Is annual salary before or after taxes?

Before taxes. The annual salary figures you see in wage conversions are gross pay, meaning everything you earn before federal income tax, state tax, local tax, Social Security (6.2%), Medicare (1.45%), health insurance, or 401(k) contributions come out. Your take-home pay on your paycheck will always be less than your gross annual salary, depending on your tax filing status and deductions.

How can I calculate my hourly rate from salary?

Divide your annual gross salary by the number of hours you work each year. On a standard 40-hour full-time schedule (2,080 hours), divide your salary by 2,080. A $60,000 salary divided by 2,080 hours works out to about $28.85 an hour. If your schedule is 45 hours a week (2,340 hours), that same $60,000 salary is worth $25.64 an hour. For our complete step-by-step calculation guide and 16-rate conversion table, see how to calculate hourly rate from salary.

Key Takeaways

Core Summary Points

  • The Master Formula: Your hourly rate times your weekly hours times your paid weeks in the year (Rate × Hours/Week × Weeks/Year).
  • The Standard Full-Time Benchmark: Full-time usually means 40 hours a week and 52 weeks a year, which adds up to 2,080 scheduled hours.
  • Impact of Unpaid Leave: Unpaid vacation or leave cuts your paid weeks and lowers your annual gross pay. Paid time off (PTO) doesn't.
  • Overtime Earnings: Eligible non-exempt hours past 40 a week pay at least 1.5× time and a half, which can lift your yearly total a lot.
  • Gross vs. Net Income: Every conversion here is gross pay, before taxes and benefits. What you actually take home depends on your own tax withholdings and deductions.

How We Calculate Annual Salary

Our standard hourly-to-annual calculation multiplies your hourly wage by the hours you work each week and the weeks you work each year. For a typical full-time schedule, that's 40 hours a week and 52 weeks a year, or 2,080 hours annually. If your schedule looks different, you can change those assumptions. Every estimate is gross pay, before payroll deductions, taxes, and contributions. For the full math behind it, see our Calculation Methodology.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The core formula is hourly rate × hours per week × paid weeks (2,080 hours for a standard full-time year).
  2. At $25 an hour, full-time gross pay is $1,000 a week, $2,000 biweekly, and about $4,333.33 a month.
  3. Unpaid weeks lower the total: two unpaid weeks bring $25 an hour down to $50,000 a year, while overtime is extra on top.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 3, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
